https://us.cnn.com/2026/09/05/politics/g.text: Greg Bovino thinks the Trump administration is weak on mass deportation. And he’ll share that message anywhere he can — even on a whiskey bottle. Months removed from his unceremonious dismissal as the public face of President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement surge, the former Border Patrol “commander-at-large” has found a new role as an anti-immigrant influencer, sharing his radical views with anyone who will listen. He regularly mixes in criticism of his former employers for what he views as their failure to live up to Trump’s mass deportation pledge. Bovino has traveled to Europe to speak with members of right-wing parties on immigration crackdowns. He has frequented far-right podcasts to amplify his uncompromising outlook on immigration enforcement, is working on a tell-all book of his time in the administration, and has lined up speaking engagements with young conservatives to share his belief that immigration is changing the fiber of this country. Bovino has also created his own whiskey label, Commander’s Choice, with bottles available to pre-order for $99 with a label that says: “Deport them all. America first.” (“It’s a fantastic drink for law enforcement,” he told CNN. “It’s keto friendly.”) His antics have irritated more than a few people in the administration along the way. The Department of Homeland Security that once gave him unprecedented power now refers to him as a “disgruntled” former employee. Those feelings go both ways. In a recent interview with Tucker Carlson, Bovino said he resents how his security detail was pulled after he retired despite the constant death threats he says he receives. “Do I think they want me dead? At this point, yes,” he told Carlson. In a series of interviews with CNN over the summer, and in podcast appearances, Bovino appears simultaneously hurt and furious over how the administration pushed him aside following the fatal shootings by federal law enforcement officers of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, two American citizens in Minneapolis. “In a nutshell, what I wanted to do is continue the push for mass deportations and the push to save America from what’s happening here in terms of immigration,” he told CNN in a recent interview. “I don’t see those mass deportations occurring the way I think they need to go.” Bovino appears to relish the controversy, dismissing criticism and maintaining that he’s not alone in his views that the administration is falling short of its immigration enforcement promises. He’s continued to draw the ire of some within the administration — he won’t immediately say who — and he said he has been told, unofficially, to knock off his public airing of grievances. “I said no — a lot more forcefully than no,” he said. A loose cannon Bovino has long been known as something of a loose cannon with a penchant for provocative antics and social media trolling. Trump himself once described Bovino as “a pretty out there kind of a guy.” (“Maybe a lot of people think I’m out there,” Bovino said. “I really don’t care.”) But to a segment of the president’s base that has become disillusioned with the administration’s more lowkey approach to immigration enforcement after the fatal shootings by federal officers of Good and Pretti earlier this year, Bovino has emerged as a leader with a clear-eyed view of what they believe is needed. Mike Howell, a visiting fellow at the conservative Heritage Foundation and the president of the Oversight Project, said Bovino is “indisputably correct” in his criticisms. “The Trump administration promised mass deportations and hasn’t delivered it yet,” Howell said. “And so, there is going to be that flank open, up until they deliver it.” “Bovino is going to have a platform and credibility until he’s proven wrong by the Trump administration actually doing mass deportations, and so whether it’s him or anybody else, the field for somebody to reclaim the issue is wide open,” Howell added. Immigration arrests, however, have increased over recent months. Immigration and Customs Enforcement took around 51,000 people into custody in August, according to a source familiar with the data, continuing an upward trend in immigration arrests and setting a new high under the second Trump administration. Still, some immigration restrictionists, including Bovino, say the administration is lagging. He says immigrants who do not integrate into American society are a bigger threat to the country than those who are criminals or terrorists. He wants a temporary moratorium on all immigration to the US. And he doesn’t just want undocumented immigrants deported — he wants those living here legally who have not assimilated into his idea of American culture to go, too. He believes more than 100 million people are living illegally in the country, which is multitudes more than even the most expansive estimates cited by anti-immigration hardliners. (The Pew Research Center estimated there were a record 14 million undocumented immigrants in the US in 2023 — the most recent year with comprehensive data.) While Bovino has his supporters, some former and current Homeland Security officials are frustrated by the attention he gets and have largely dismissed the ongoing public commentary. The critics include those who support Bovino’s overall goal of reducing the population of undocumented immigrants in the country, but who were not impressed by the way the operations were handled earlier this year in cities like Minneapolis. “Secretary Noem was pursuing this strategy of theatrical enforcement that he was kind of the face of, and there was no way that was going to be sustainable,” said Mark Krikorian, the executive director of the Center for Immigration Studies, which supports reduced immigration. “It hurt the president, and it hurt his agenda of reducing the illegal population. Part of the reason the administration is not deporting as many people as it would like to see is precisely because of the strategy that Bovino was the face of, that undermined the political support for deporting illegals,” he added. Bovino’s decades-long career with Border Patrol ended earlier this year amid an internal investigation. According to government files, which were first reported by the Chicago Tribune and posted on the Customs and Border Protection website, Bovino was contacted by investigators on March 2 regarding “allegations of misconduct,” that were reported to the agency, including allegations that he had made antisemitic comments. Bovino has denied that the comments in question were intended to be antisemitic. He was also accused of lying about events during an immigration operation in Chicago, raising questions about his credibility, according to the files. Bovino retired later that month. The results of that investigation were unclear. A CBP spokesperson said the agency “does not comment on matters regarding personnel who are no longer with the agency.” Bovino told Border Hawk that he was forced to retire and claimed that CBP’s Office of Professional Responsibility was weaponized against him. ‘We surrendered’ Bovino nurses some grudges about how his time in federal government ended, arguing that he was kneecapped from implementing the “total spectrum immigration enforcement” that he had hoped for, and which he is calling for now, before his vision could fully be realized. “We surrendered in Minnesota,” he said. “We didn’t get there yet because it was cut off, as you know, very suddenly, and almost without explanation.” He sees the upcoming midterm elections as a way to pressure the administration to double down on its immigration crackdown — in his vision. Bovino is careful to avoid criticizing the president directly, but said he believes Trump is surrounded by ineffective officials who are more concerned by optics than results, citing White House border czar Tom Homan, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, and US Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott. “If I hurt someone’s feelings — some feckless government bureaucrat — because I’m telling the truth and they can’t handle the truth, well they can kiss my ass, by God,” Bovino said. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis broadly defended the administration’s immigration policies in a statement, saying that more than 3 million undocumented immigrants have left the country either through deportation or departing on their own. She also defended Homan. “The American people are deeply appreciative of Tom Homan’s work and can rest easy knowing someone with a proven track record is working to deliver on the President’s promise to deport a historic number of illegal aliens,” Bis said. A DHS spokesperson said “disgruntled former employees” were “welcome to criticize their nation’s leadership.” Asked by CNN at a press conference in June about Bovino’s criticisms over Mullin’s leadership of his agency, the secretary tersely dismissed him. “I’ve never met the guy,” Mullin said. “He’s irrelevant to me. I don’t know who he is.” A book and a whiskey bottle Bovino has since moved back to his home state of North Carolina and frequently visits east Tennessee. He’s writing a book that he describes as a “book of truth, leadership, and philosophy,” beaming into interviews and fielding speaking engagements. Recently, he revisited one of the locations of his operations, leading to a confrontation between him and a local business owner. He’s trying to prove a point. And also trying to monetize it. “It’s all toward the same end. Are we going to bring attention to what the problem is? If I can use a whiskey label to do that, if I can use the podcast to do that, if I can go to a bakery?” he said. Camden Ford, co-owner of Timber Creek Distillery based in Florida and maker of Bovino’s new whiskey, told CNN he connected with him by way of Bovino’s sister. “I’m happy to work with Greg if he wants to do a whiskey. I’m happy to work with anybody. I don’t really care about their politics,” he told CNN, adding that the distillery works with dozens of customers on private labels. The two have discussed a series that would include a bottle for each of the operations Bovino led over the last year. “He may be controversial, but it may be the thing that sells his whiskey for him,” Ford said. The attention is also making Bovino a draw to the right-wing speaking circuit. He appeared at an event hosted by the group Save Heritage Indiana in August and is scheduled to appear before the New York Young Republicans Club later this month. Globe-trotting and eyeing 2028 Bovino is also spreading his message abroad. In Portugal, he gave an interview with a far-right French publication in which he cited Nazi General Erwin Rommel, along with American figures like Gen. George S. Patton and FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover, as people who became the faces of large movements because of the unique set of circumstances they faced. (Bovino told CNN his answer had “nothing to do with Rommel, his style [or] his beliefs” and that he only brought him up to relate to the European publication that interviewed him.) In June, Bovino spoke at another conference in Romania, where he posted a picture of himself in front of the tomb of Vlad the Impaler, the former Wallachian prince whose bloodthirsty methods while resisting an Ottoman invasion gave him his gruesome name. “He was sort of their original Border Patrol,” Bovino said. “He said, ‘You know, we’ve had enough of these Ottomans coming in and doing terrible things to our citizens. I’m going to try to do something about it.’ And obviously, back in the medieval times, things are a little different than they are now.” In May, a group of political operatives set up a website — along with a donation link — encouraging Bovino to mount a presidential campaign in 2028. Bovino said he was unaware of that specific effort until it began and told CNN that he hasn’t seen a penny of any of the donations made on that website. (Jacob Engels, one of the operatives who established the site, said Bovino was involved in the effort early on but then abandoned it.) Bovino said young Republicans frequently ask him to run for president, that he finds the idea “very, very, very interesting” and that he is keeping his options open. This article has been updated with additional information.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Police are seen around the premises of Poland's constitutional court after its head was suspended in Warsaw, Poland, on Friday. Photograph: Agata Grzybowska/Anadolu/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Police are seen around the premises of Poland's constitutional court after its head was suspended in Warsaw, Poland, on Friday. Photograph: Agata Grzybowska/Anadolu/Getty Images Poland Riot police deployed to Poland’s constitutional court after judge suspended President Karol Nawrocki seen struggling to gain entry to court building in Warsaw amid long-running row over the court’s legitimacy Jakub Krupa Sat 31 Oct 2026 00.27 EDT Last modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 02.37 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Riot police were locked in a tense standoff with protesters outside Poland’s constitutional court on Friday night after its top judge was suspended in the latest escalation in a decade-long dispute over the court’s legal status. The clashes followed a controversial decision by a group of government-appointed judges to suspend the court’s contested president, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, amid disagreements over the bench’s legitimacy. The move prompted a furious reaction from the rightwing opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, with its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, condemning what he claimed was an “assault” on the court. The court frequently ruled in favour of Polish legislation over EU law and the European Union accused Poland’s highest court of being too close to the nationalist political power of the time. Poland’s ascent from communist state to top 20 economy reverses the brain drain Read more The PiS-backed conservative president, Karol Nawrocki, a close ally of Donald Trump, turned his plane around en route to a state visit in Senegal to return to Warsaw and intervene at the court on Friday night. Hundreds of protesters – including opposition MPs – gathered outside the building to show their support for the suspended judges. Police said they detained three people after some protesters breached the tribunal’s fence and others threw objects at officers. Shortly before 1am on Saturday, Nawrocki appeared outside the court and made his way through the police cordon , with one video showing the president tussling with security and other judges to force his entry into the building. As of 4am local time, the president remained inside the building. In a clip posted online , Nawrocki was heard saying the government appointees “were not judges of the constitutional court”. In a statement read out on his behalf outside the court at 5am, Nawrocki criticised “a violation of Poland’s constitutional order”, saying “a constitutional body was seized by force”. He called for security forces to leave the premises. The latest clash is likely to further polarise the country, setting the scene for a dramatic showdown in next year’s parliamentary election, with polls showing the populist-right with a chance to return to power. View image in fullscreen Police are seen around the premises of Poland’s top court amid protests over its head’s suspension in Warsaw, Poland. Photograph: Agata Grzybowska/Anadolu/Getty Images The court has been at the centre of a dispute dating back to 2015, when the outgoing centrist and the incoming rightwing governments moved in quick succession with legally questionable moves to stack the bench with their appointees. The dispute over the appointments paralysed the court , followed by further attempts to cripple it during the PiS’s eight years of illiberal rule marred by clashes with the EU over the rule of law. Since returning to power in 2023, Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, has repeatedly pledged to reverse controversial reforms as he sought to mend relations with Brussels , while refusing to recognise the court’s legitimacy in the current form. However, his efforts have been thwarted by opposition-aligned presidents who used their veto powers and expansive interpretations of their powers to block reforms. In the latest twist this year, Nawrocki, who unexpectedly won last year’s presidential election against Tusk’s candidate, refused to swear in five judges elected by the current parliament, further complicating the legal situation. Earlier this month, the Council of Europe’s advisory body on the rule of law, the Venice Commission, said the president’s refusal should not prevent judges from taking up their posts. On Friday night, a group of judges elected by the current majority moved to suspend Święczkowski, a former minister under PiS, and seize procedural control of the court. Anna Korwin-Piotrowska – who is one of the five judges not accepted by Nawrocki – said she had assumed the top position, citing the longest experience in the judiciary. View image in fullscreen Disputed chief justice Bogdan Swięczkowski presents his judicial document to reporters in front of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw, Poland. Photograph: Radek Pietruszka/EPA Experts are deeply divided in their opinion on the legality of the judge’s suspension. Marcin Matczak, a prominent law expert and outspoken critic of PiS, said he “did not think he would ever end up defending” Święczkowski, but believed the legal basis for his suspension was “non-existent”. Separately, justice minister Waldemar Żurek said he had asked for Święczkowski and deputy chief Sochański to be stripped of their legal immunity to face prosecution for obstructing the court’s work. View image in fullscreen Polish president Karol Nawrocki arrives at the constitutional tribunal in Warsaw, Poland. Photograph: Dawid Żuchowicz/Agencja Wyborcza.pl/Reuters Despite criticism, Tusk insisted that “restoring the rule of law is our duty.” “After years of PiS’s lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way,” he argued. Earlier this month, he pledged “the court will begin its work in accordance with the constitution, whether people like it or not.” Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski told reporters on the margins of a G20 meeting in Atlanta that “the constitutional tribunal was politicised under the previous government.” “What is happening has the purpose of allowing the majority of duly elected judges to make the tribunal function again,” he said. Opposition leaders and the court’s social media account accused the government of carrying out a judicial “a coup d’état”. Several European far-right figures, including Britain’s Nigel Farage, Liz Truss and the Netherlands’ Geert Wilders, also condemned the move. US ambassador to Poland Tom Rose said in a post on X: “The events unfolding tonight … are very serious.” “Both sides offer sharply different accounts of what happened and why,” he said. “Whatever the facts ultimately establish, thousands gathering outside the tribunal make an already dangerous situation more combustible. The last thing Poland needs is a confrontation that spirals into something far worse.” Explore more on these topics Poland Europe Donald Tusk Karol Nawrocki news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Beállítom Leszállt szombaton a belarusz Gomel város repülőtéren mind a négy repülőgép, amikkel az orosz-ukrán fronton lévő, szétlőtt Oleski város lakosait menekítették ki – írta a Reuters , a belarusz állami médiára és egy magas rangú ukrán tisztviselőre hivatkozva. „Az utolsó, negyedik gép is leszállt Gomelben, pár óra múlva az Oleskiből evakuált összes ukrán állampolgár, az ukrán delegációval együtt ukrán területen lesz” – mondta szombat délelőtt David Arahamija ukrán parlamenti képviselő, Ukrajna fő béketárgyalója. A lakosokat pénteken kezdték el kimenekíteni , aztán, hogy kedd hajnalban az orosz és az ukrán erők is felfüggesztették a harcokat a dél-ukrajnai városnál. A tűzszünet állítólag Melania Trump amerikai first lady közvetítésével jött létre. A tűzszünetet egyik fél sem szegte meg. A szétlőtt városból több száz éhező ember hoztak ki, akik nem tudtak egyből a mindössze öt kilométerre lévő ukrán ellenőrzés alatt területre menni. Először buszokkal az oroszországi Anapa városában szállították őket, majd onnan repülőgépekkel a belarusz-ukrán határhoz közel lévő Gomelbe. Onnan újra buszra szállnak, hogy Ukrajnába jussanak. Szétlőtt város A Dnyeper folyó partján fekvő Oleskiben hónapok óta súlyos élelmiszer- és gyógyszerhiány alakult ki. A folyó választja el az ukrán erőket a várost megszállás alatt tartó orosz csapatoktól. A Herszon megyei városban nincs áram, fűtés és vezetékes víz. A városból kivezető utakat elaknásították, az út mentén kiégett autók sorakoznak, a drónok blokád alatt tartják a települést. Az egykor 24 ezer lakosú város a Dnyeper folyó orosz megszállás alatti oldalán fekszik, pont szemben az ukrán területen lévő nagyvárossal, Herszonnal. Herszont a háború kezdete óta hevesen támadják az oroszok a Dnyeper túlpartjáról, ráadásul a frontvonalnak számító folyópartot is hevesen bombázzák , hogy megakadályozzák az orosz területen élő civilek átszökését az ukrán oldalra. Az Oleskiben élők tehát a háború kezdete óta szó szerint két tűz között ragadtak. A városban kialakult helyzetről és a tűzszünetről ebben a cikkben írtunk részletesen .
